citation: Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology (JCGM). International vocabulary of metrology - Basic and general concepts and associated terms (VIM), 3rd edition. JCGM 200:2012 (2008 version with minor corrections). BIPM; 2012.
venue_and_status: JCGM guidance document published by BIPM for the JCGM member organizations; current published edition on 2026-10-12 (VIM4 is at second committee draft, 2023 documents on the JCGM-WG2 page); bilingual PDF read in full for the cited entries
problem: Common vocabulary of measurement
method: International terminology standard
main_result: Entries read verbatim: 2.3 measurand (p.17); 2.6 measurement procedure (p.18); 2.15 measurement precision (p.22); 2.20 repeatability condition (p.23); 2.21 repeatability, 2.22 intermediate precision condition (Note 1: changes can include new calibrations, calibrators, operators and measuring systems), 2.24 reproducibility condition (Note 1: different measuring systems may use different measurement procedures) (p.24); 2.25 reproducibility (p.25); 2.39 calibration (Note 1: may be an additive or multiplicative correction of the indication) (p.28); 2.46 metrological comparability (p.31); 2.47 metrological compatibility of measurement results (p.32); 3.2 measuring system (p.34); 4.21 instrumental drift (p.43)
relevance: Primary source for the Discussion's 'change of instrument' sentence and for a VIM-consistent definition of version compatibility (2.47) and of the measurement conditions under which baseline and follow-up are obtained (2.20 vs 2.24)
not_established: Says nothing about software or trained models; treating a model version as part of the 'measuring system' (3.2) or 'measurement procedure' (2.6) is the authors' interpretation; 'cross-calibration' is not a VIM term

citation: Kessler LG, Barnhart HX, Buckler AJ, Choudhury KR, Kondratovich MV, Toledano A, Guimaraes AR, Filice R, Zhang Z, Sullivan DC; QIBA Terminology Working Group. The emerging science of quantitative imaging biomarkers terminology and definitions for scientific studies and regulatory submissions. Stat Methods Med Res 2015;24(1):9-26.
venue_and_status: Statistical Methods in Medical Research, published (OnlineFirst 11 June 2014; issue February 2015). Read: OnlineFirst version of record (pages 1-18) from the DukeSpace repository copy; page numbers differ from the issue
problem: Inconsistent terminology for quantitative imaging biomarkers (QIBs)
method: Consensus terminology adapted from VIM and ISO documents, with examples
main_result: Repeatability = measurement precision under repeatability conditions; reproducibility = precision under reproducibility conditions [VIM 2.25]; '95% precision limit' = 2.77s where s is the within-subject SD; 'it is called a RDC if s corresponds to the wSD under reproducibility conditions' and RC under repeatability conditions; recommends precision profiles and explicit statement of measurement conditions; lists 'scanner software changes' among within-site sources of variation
relevance: QIBA terminology for RC, RDC, wSD, wCV and precision profiles, needed to name a version-compatibility metric consistently
not_established: Its gloss that reproducibility 'still requires the same measurement procedure' is narrower than VIM 2.24 Note 1; body text cites VIM 2.21 for the repeatability condition and 2.16 for precision (VIM numbers are 2.20 and 2.15); no metric for software or model version changes

citation: Raunig DL, McShane LM, Pennello G, Gatsonis C, Carson PL, Voyvodic JT, Wahl RL, Kurland BF, Schwarz AJ, Gonen M, Zahlmann G, Kondratovich MV, O'Donnell K, Petrick N, Cole PE, Garra B, Sullivan DC. Quantitative imaging biomarkers: a review of statistical methods for technical performance assessment. Stat Methods Med Res 2015;24(1):27-67.
venue_and_status: Statistical Methods in Medical Research, published; NIH author manuscript (PMC5574197) read
problem: Statistical methods for bias, linearity, repeatability and reproducibility of QIBs
method: Methodological review with worked examples
data: Simulated and example data incl. QIBA 3A phantom volumes
main_result: RC = 1.96 x sqrt(2 s_w^2) = 2.77 s_w, 'the least significant difference between two repeated measurements taken under identical conditions'; LOA = [-RC, RC]; wCV = sigma_w/mu and, for log-normal data, wCV = sqrt(exp(sigma_ln^2) - 1), approx. sigma_ln; sigma^2_reproducibility = sigma^2_repeatability + sigma^2_between-factors; RDC = 2.77 sqrt(sigma_delta^2 + sigma_gammadelta^2 + sigma_eps^2), conditions may be instruments, readers/reviewers or algorithms; test whether reproducibility variation exceeds repeatability (H0: sigma_delta^2 = sigma_gammadelta^2 = 0)
relevance: Variance decomposition that maps onto a systematic version shift (condition main effect) plus lesion-level version disagreement (case-by-condition interaction); basis for RDC/RC-type compatibility ratios
not_established: Conditions are modelled as random; no treatment of sequential software versions or of change measured across conditions; quotes are from the accepted manuscript

citation: Sullivan DC, Obuchowski NA, Kessler LG, Raunig DL, Gatsonis C, Huang EP, Kondratovich M, McShane LM, Reeves AP, Barboriak DP, Guimaraes AR, Wahl RL; RSNA-QIBA Metrology Working Group. Metrology standards for quantitative imaging biomarkers. Radiology 2015;277(3):813-825.
venue_and_status: Radiology, published; PMC4666097 HTML text read (tables are images and were not read)
problem: Terminology and study design for QIB technical performance
method: Consensus review
main_result: Repeatability = precision 'with identical or near-identical conditions'; reproducibility = precision 'when location, operator, measuring system, or other factors differ'; 'Examples of image analysis factors that may vary include scanner hardware changes, scanner software changes, ...'; 'if the same subject will be measured at times t1 and t2 by different operators, then both within- and between-operator components of variance will have an effect on what measured amount of change can be reliably interpreted as a true biological change'; log transformation can remove dependence of bias/precision on the measurand
relevance: Radiology-level metrology reference stating that between-condition variance enters change when timepoints are measured under different conditions
not_established: No quantitative treatment of software versions; tables not read

citation: Obuchowski NA. Interpreting change in quantitative imaging biomarkers. Acad Radiol 2018;25(3):372-379.
venue_and_status: Academic Radiology, published; NIH author manuscript (PMC5834376) read
problem: Cut-points separating real change from measurement error
method: Monte Carlo comparison of three RC estimation approaches under five error scenarios
main_result: RC = 1.96 x sqrt(2 sigma^2), 'the least significant difference between two repeat measurements taken under identical conditions'; log approach RC_ln = 1.96 x sqrt(2 sigma_ln^2) with asymmetric back-transformed limits exp(-RC_ln)-1 and exp(+RC_ln)-1; log and wCV approaches perform similarly when error is proportional to the true value; recommends precision profiles (lung nodule wCV decreases with size)
relevance: Log-scale (ratio) change thresholds and asymmetric limits appropriate for volume change
not_established: Repeatability only; no between-system or between-version component

citation: Obuchowski NA, Barnhart HX, Buckler AJ, Pennello G, Wang XF, Kalpathy-Cramer J, Kim HJ, Reeves AP; Case Example Working Group. Statistical issues in the comparison of quantitative imaging biomarker algorithms using pulmonary nodule volume as an example. Stat Methods Med Res 2015;24(1):107-140.
venue_and_status: Statistical Methods in Medical Research, published; NIH author manuscript (PMC4263699) read
problem: Applying algorithm-comparison statistics to nodule volume and volume change
method: Worked analyses of three studies; mixed-effects reproducibility models
data: Phantom bias/repeatability study; QIBA 3A phantom challenge; VOLCANO'09 (9 zero-change and 9 change nodules, 6 algorithms)
main_result: Precision of change from single-timepoint precision s(Y0-Yt) = sqrt(s(Y0)^2 + s(Yt)^2 - 2 r s(Y0) s(Yt)); 'reproducibility interval' for two measurements under different conditions with a fixed condition effect, RI = delta_hat +/- 1.96 sqrt(V_dnew + V_delta_hat) (asymmetric); 95% CI for true change across the fixed condition change = (d_new - delta_hat) +/- 1.96 sqrt(V_dnew + V_delta_hat), illustrated for slice thickness 0.8 vs 5 mm; TDI(90%) between algorithms' proportional change measurements 16.39%
relevance: Closest formal method for change measured with a different (fixed) condition at each timepoint; the adjustment removes only the fixed effect, leaving case-by-condition variance (cf. scalar recalibration vs reprocessing)
not_established: Condition studied is slice thickness, not a software or model version; phantom-based; no deep learning

citation: QIBA CT Volumetry Biomarker Committee. CT Tumor Volume Change for Advanced Disease (CTV-AD) Profile. Quantitative Imaging Biomarkers Alliance. Profile Stage: Clinically Feasible. July 21, 2022. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1148/qiba/20220721
venue_and_status: QIBA Profile, Stage 3 Clinically Feasible (streamlined), 2022 edition (re-publication of the 2018 Technically Confirmed profile); listed as current on the QIBA wiki Profiles and CT Volumetry committee pages (accessed 2026-10-12); 32-page PDF read in full
problem: Reliable measurement of CT tumour volume change in advanced disease
method: Consensus profile: claims, actor checklists, assessment procedures
data: Claims derived from lung data (QIBA groundwork and literature; RIDER coffee-break data used for conformance testing)
main_result: Change Detection Claim: true change with 95% confidence if measured change is larger than 24%, 29% or 39% for longest in-plane diameter 50-100, 35-49 or 10-34 mm; Repeatability Claim wCV 0.085, 0.103, 0.141; requires the same Image Analysis Tool and the same Radiologist at both timepoints and re-processing of the first timepoint if it was processed by a different tool or radiologist; Table B-1 (informative) minimum detectable change, same scanner and radiologist, same vs different analysis tool: 8% vs 37% (>50 mm), 14% vs 60% (35-49 mm), 28% vs 75% (10-34 mm)
relevance: Reference scale for volume change and the standards-body precedent for reprocessing the baseline when the analysis tool differs
not_established: Claims are lung-only ('the expected performance has not yet been determined' for kidneys, liver, lymph nodes); claims are a committee hypothesis not yet substantiated by conformant studies; 'version' of the image analysis tool is not mentioned (only 'tool'; checklist records Make/Model/Version); Table B-1 values are not claims and assume untested additivity; text cites a 'Table 2-1' and 'Table B-2' that do not exist in this edition
code_or_data: Conformance test data on QIDW (RIDER Lung CT; QIBA Lung Collection; LungMan DRO)

citation: QIBA CT Volumetry Biomarker Committee. Small Lung Nodule Volume Assessment and Monitoring in Low Dose CT Screening, Clinically Feasible Profile. Quantitative Imaging Biomarkers Alliance. December 19, 2023. Available from: https://doi.org/10.1148/qiba/20231219
venue_and_status: QIBA Profile, Stage 3 Clinically Feasible (cover page); listed on the QIBA wiki with date 19 Dec 2023 and DOI; the cover's citation line still reads 'Publicly Reviewed Draft'; PDF read (claims, Table 1, section 3.10)
problem: Volume and volume change of 6-10 mm solid lung nodules in low-dose CT screening
method: Consensus profile
data: Clinical trial data, theoretical analysis, simulations, literature
main_result: Table 1 CV: 6 mm 0.29, 7 mm 0.23, 8 mm 0.19, 9 mm 0.16, 10 mm 0.14; minimum detectable difference (2.77 x CV) 80.3%, 63.7%, 52.6%, 44.3%, 38.8%; section 3.10.1: 'different versions of the same program or its components may change its performance, a nodule being evaluated for change must be analyzed at both time points with the same software program (manufacturer, model, and version)'; 3.10.2: 'Shall use the same Image Analysis Tool (manufacturer, model, version) for measurements at all time points'
relevance: Explicit standards-body rule requiring one software version across timepoints; small-lesion reference scale
not_established: Lung nodules in screening; claims not fully substantiated; Table 1 volume for 7 mm (154 mm3) is inconsistent with a 7-mm sphere (about 180 mm3, as in the profile's own example)

citation: Athelogou M, Kim HJ, Dima A, Obuchowski N, Peskin A, Gavrielides MA, Petrick N, Saiprasad G, Colditz D, Beaumont H, Oubel E, Tan Y, Zhao B, Kuhnigk JM, Moltz JH, Orieux G, Gillies RJ, Gu Y, Mantri N, Goldmacher G, Zhang L, Vega E, Bloom M, Jarecha R, Soza G, Tietjen C, Takeguchi T, Yamagata H, Peterson S, Masoud O, Buckler AJ. Algorithm variability in the estimation of lung nodule volume from phantom CT scans: results of the QIBA 3A public challenge. Acad Radiol 2016;23(8):940-952.
venue_and_status: Academic Radiology, published; NIST author manuscript (PMC6237094) read
problem: Bias and precision of many volumetry algorithms
method: Public challenge; 10 participants' semi-automated algorithms
data: FDA anthropomorphic phantom: synthetic nodules 5-40 mm, 5 shapes, 5 densities, 0.8 and 5 mm slices
main_result: QIBA-compliant nodules: RC 9.0% with the same algorithm vs RDC 22.1% of average volume across algorithms (Table 7); by nominal size, wCV 4.52%, 2.27%, 0.82% and RDC 46.5%, 32.1%, 8.0% for 10-12, 20 and 40 mm
relevance: Published magnitude of how much changing the measuring algorithm inflates variability relative to repeatability
not_established: Phantom data likely underestimate clinical variability; different vendors' algorithms rather than versions of one model

citation: McNitt-Gray MF, Kim GH, Zhao B, Schwartz LH, Clunie D, Cohen K, Petrick N, Fenimore C, Lu ZQJ, Buckler AJ. Determining the variability of lesion size measurements from CT patient data sets acquired under 'no change' conditions. Transl Oncol 2015;8(1):55-64.
venue_and_status: Translational Oncology, published, open access (CC BY-NC-ND); full text read
problem: Lesion-size variability under no-change conditions and effect of reading paradigm
method: Five radiologists; independent vs locked sequential reads; 1D, 2D and semi-automated 3D
data: RIDER coffee-break data: 32 NSCLC patients scanned twice within 15 min on the same scanner
main_result: Semi-automated volume, percent change (mean +/- SD, pooled over readers and lesions): 23.4 +/- 105% for independent reads vs 7.4 +/- 44.2% for locked sequential reads; proportional change 5.5 +/- 39.2% vs 2.2 +/- 25.5%
relevance: Processing both timepoints together sharply reduced change variability, the reader-side analogue of measuring both timepoints with one model version
not_established: Reader-edited volumes; mean +/- SD is not an RC; one scanner

citation: Bland JM, Altman DG. Statistical methods for assessing agreement between two methods of clinical measurement. Lancet 1986;327(8476):307-310.
venue_and_status: The Lancet, published; author-hosted HTML reproduction (by permission of the Lancet, with a small numerical correction) read
problem: Agreement between two measurement methods
method: Limits of agreement and difference-versus-mean plots
main_result: Limits of agreement d +/- 2s; 'If the differences are proportional to the mean, a logarithmic transformation should yield' a constant scatter; antilogged limits are a dimensionless ratio (example 0.80 to 1.27)
relevance: Origin of limits of agreement and of log-ratio limits for volume
not_established: No longitudinal or change setting

citation: Bland JM, Altman DG. Measuring agreement in method comparison studies. Stat Methods Med Res 1999;8(2):135-160.
venue_and_status: Statistical Methods in Medical Research, published; abstract read (two DOIs registered; PubMed uses the SAGE DOI)
problem: Method comparison
method: Limits of agreement and extensions
main_result: 95% LoA = mean difference +/- 1.96 SD of differences; extensions for magnitude-dependent differences (log transformation; regression), comparison with each method's repeatability, replicated data including a changing underlying value, nonparametric approach
relevance: Standard citation for between-version bias and limits of agreement on a log scale
not_established: Full text not read

citation: Euser AM, Dekker FW, le Cessie S. A practical approach to Bland-Altman plots and variation coefficients for log transformed variables. J Clin Epidemiol 2008;61(10):978-982.
venue_and_status: Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, published; abstract read
problem: Reproducibility indices for log-transformed variables
method: Derivation and worked example
main_result: CVs derived from the SD of log-transformed measurements; limits of agreement computed on the log scale and back-transformed to the original scale
relevance: Practical reporting of log-scale limits as percentages
not_established: Full text not read

citation: Barnhart HX, Kosinski AS, Haber MJ. Assessing individual agreement. J Biopharm Stat 2007;17(4):697-719.
venue_and_status: Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics, published; abstract read
problem: When can methods be used interchangeably?
method: Individual equivalence based on FDA individual-bioequivalence moment criteria; individual equivalence coefficient and coefficient of individual agreement (CIA)
main_result: 'interchangeability is established only if individual measurements from different methods are similar to replicated measurements from the same method'; proposes IEC and CIA
relevance: Scaled compatibility index comparing between-version disagreement with within-version disagreement
not_established: Needs replicate measurements by each method; not imaging-specific; full text not read

citation: Haber M, Barnhart HX. A general approach to evaluating agreement between two observers or methods of measurement from quantitative data with replicated measurements. Stat Methods Med Res 2008;17(2):151-169.
venue_and_status: Statistical Methods in Medical Research, published (online 2007); abstract read
problem: Agreement coefficients for fixed methods
method: Disagreement functions; nonparametric estimation
main_result: Inter-method coefficients compare disagreement between methods with disagreement between replicates of the same method; disagreement functions: mean squared, mean absolute and mean relative difference; with or without a reference method
relevance: Relative-difference version suits ratio-scale volume
not_established: Full text not read

citation: Haber M, Gao J, Barnhart HX. Evaluation of agreement between measurement methods from data with matched repeated measurements via the coefficient of individual agreement. J Data Sci 2010;8(3):457-469.
venue_and_status: Journal of Data Science, published; NIH author manuscript (PMC2907262) read
problem: Agreement between methods with matched repeated measurements
method: Mixed-model estimation of the CIA
main_result: CIA without a reference: psi = [MSD(Y1,Y1') + MSD(Y2,Y2')] / [2 MSD(Y1,Y2)]; agreement suggested as acceptable only if CIA > 0.8; condition-specific CIAs when disagreement varies across conditions or time
relevance: Exact definition for a scaled version-compatibility index
not_established: The 0.8 threshold is the authors' suggestion; non-imaging examples

citation: International Society for Clinical Densitometry. Official Positions 2023 (Adult). ISCD; approved 24 August 2023. https://iscd.org/official-positions-2023/ (accessed 12 October 2026).
venue_and_status: Professional society official positions, web document ('Supersedes all prior Official Positions publications'); page read
problem: Longitudinal BMD monitoring across DXA systems
method: Consensus positions
main_result: LSC from facility precision; when an entire system is changed, cross-calibrate in patients and use the inter-system LSC; 'Inter-system quantitative comparisons can only be made if cross-calibration is performed on each skeletal site commonly measured'; 'If a cross-calibration assessment is not performed, no quantitative comparison to the prior machine can be made. Consequently, a new baseline BMD and intra-system LSC should be established.'; 'Do not apply an LSC or report BMD change between instruments that are not cross-calibrated.'
relevance: Clinical precedent that a change of measuring system breaks longitudinal comparability unless bridged (cross-calibration) or re-baselined; also an operational inter-system change threshold
not_established: Hardware/system replacement in DXA; software version changes not addressed in these positions; a DXA baseline cannot be re-measured retrospectively, unlike re-analysis of a stored CT

citation: Jankowski LG, Warner S, Gaither K, Lenchik L, Fan B, Lu Y, Shepherd J. Cross-calibration, least significant change and quality assurance in multiple dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scanner environments: 2019 ISCD official position. J Clin Densitom 2019;22(4):472-483.
venue_and_status: Journal of Clinical Densitometry, published; abstract read
problem: LSC and cross-calibration with multiple DXA scanners
method: Task-force literature review and positions
main_result: Three new positions on LSC across scanners of the same model, different models and different manufacturers, and on phantom cross-calibration
relevance: Peer-reviewed source for the ISCD cross-calibration positions
not_established: Full text not read

citation: Wong JCH, Griffiths MR. Comparative evaluation of the DPX and DPX-IQ Lunar densitometer systems following software upgrade. J Clin Densitom 2002;5(2):199-205.
venue_and_status: Journal of Clinical Densitometry, published; abstract read
problem: Effect of a densitometry analysis-software upgrade on BMD
method: Reanalysis of 200 data files per site with the upgraded software (improved femur edge detection)
main_result: No change at spine, radius or total body; femoral neck BMD 95% limits of agreement -0.057 to 0.063 g/cm2, which 'magnifies the long-term precision error and alters the usual confidence limits for interpretation of true change'; reanalysis of old files with the new software recommended so longitudinal change can be assessed
relevance: Direct precedent for re-measuring baselines after an analysis-software upgrade (overlaps T2)
not_established: Abstract only; DXA, single upgrade

citation: Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute. User Evaluation of Acceptability of a Reagent Lot Change. 2nd ed. CLSI guideline EP26. CLSI; 2022.
venue_and_status: CLSI guideline, second edition, published 27 April 2022, replaces EP26-A (2013); publisher's product page (abstract, overview, scope) read
problem: Verification of a new reagent lot
method: Two-stage protocol with patient samples and a predefined critical difference
main_result: Protocol 'for evaluating the consistency of patient sample results when a new analytical reagent lot replaces a reagent lot currently in use', for quantitative/continuous-scale procedures; setup stage fixes medically acceptable differences and risks once, then each new lot is evaluated
relevance: Laboratory precedent: each change of a measuring-system component is bridged with patient samples against a predefined acceptance limit
not_established: Document text beyond the product page not read (paywalled)

citation: Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute. Verification of Comparability of Patient Results Within One Health Care System. 2nd ed. CLSI guideline EP31. CLSI; 2025.
venue_and_status: CLSI guideline, second edition, published 25 September 2025, replaces EP31-A-IR (2012); product page (abstract, scope) read
problem: Comparability of patient results across instruments in a health system
method: Verification protocol (range test) and handling of noncomparability
main_result: Verifies comparability of quantitative results for individual patients between instruments (different manufacturers, models, or units of one model); also usable after instrument component changes or maintenance
relevance: Laboratory precedent for verifying patient-level comparability when the measuring system differs
not_established: Document text beyond the product page not read

citation: Thompson S, Chesher D. Lot-to-lot variation. Clin Biochem Rev 2018;39(2):51-60.
venue_and_status: Clinical Biochemist Reviews, published; abstract read (PMC6223607 XML contained no body text)
problem: Reagent and calibrator lot-to-lot variation
method: Narrative review
main_result: Native patient samples preferred (QC material often not commutable); 'current protocols (including the CLSI protocol) will not detect cumulative shifts between reagent lots'; moving patient averages suggested
relevance: Analogy for cumulative drift across successive model updates when each is checked only against its predecessor
not_established: Abstract only; laboratory assays

citation: Kalpathy-Cramer J, Zhao B, Goldgof D, Gu Y, Wang X, Yang H, Tan Y, Gillies R, Napel S. A comparison of lung nodule segmentation algorithms: methods and results from a multi-institutional study. J Digit Imaging 2016;29(4):476-487.
venue_and_status: Journal of Digital Imaging, published; abstract read (PMC4942386 XML restricted)
problem: Repeatability, reproducibility and bias of lung nodule segmentation algorithms
method: Three institutions' algorithms, three runs each; overlap and volume metrics
data: 52 tumours in 41 CT volumes from TCIA incl. 12 phantom nodules
main_result: Overlap higher within than between algorithms; volume bias differed; most accurate algorithms not most repeatable; 'considerable differences between algorithms ... underscoring the recommendation that the same software be used at all time points in longitudinal studies'
relevance: Supports the same-software rule and that accuracy and precision diverge
not_established: Abstract only; no version updates

citation: Gietema HA, Schaefer-Prokop CM, Mali WP, Groenewegen G, Prokop M. Pulmonary nodules: interscan variability of semiautomated volume measurements with multisection CT - influence of inspiration level, nodule size, and segmentation performance. Radiology 2007;245(3):888-894.
venue_and_status: Radiology, published; abstract read
problem: Interscan precision of semi-automated nodule volumetry
method: Two low-dose CTs with patient repositioning; Bland-Altman
data: 20 patients with lung metastases; 218 solid nodules of 16.4-472.7 mm3
main_result: 95% limits of the interscan volume difference -21.2% to 23.8% (mean 1.3%); segmentation the most important contributor
relevance: Repeat-scan reference scale for small lesions (about 0.02-0.5 mL)
not_established: Lung metastases; one commercial package; abstract only

citation: Wormanns D, Kohl G, Klotz E, Marheine A, Beyer F, Heindel W, Diederich S. Volumetric measurements of pulmonary nodules at multi-row detector CT: in vivo reproducibility. Eur Radiol 2004;14(1):86-92.
venue_and_status: European Radiology, published; abstract read
problem: In vivo precision of nodule volumetry
method: Two consecutive low-dose scans within 10 min; Bland-Altman
data: 151 nodules (2.2-20.5 mm) in 10 patients with pulmonary metastases
main_result: 95% LoA -20.4% to 21.9% (all), -19.3% to 20.4% (<10 mm); same-scan intraobserver -3.9 to 5.7%, interobserver -5.5 to 6.6%
relevance: Small-lesion repeat-scan reference scale; same-image re-measurement variability far below scan-rescan variability
not_established: Lung metastases; one software; abstract only

citation: Jirapatnakul A, Yip R, Myers KJ, Cai S, Henschke CI, Yankelevitz D. Assessing the impact of nodule features and software algorithm on pulmonary nodule measurement uncertainty for nodules sized 20 mm or less. Quant Imaging Med Surg 2024;14(7):5057-5071.
venue_and_status: Quantitative Imaging in Medicine and Surgery, published; abstract read
problem: Repeat-scan uncertainty of small-nodule volume by algorithm
method: 4-6 repeated CTs during CT-guided biopsy; two automated algorithms
data: 107 solid nodules of 20 mm or less
main_result: Median per-nodule CV 4.6% vs 8.7% for the two algorithms (P<0.001); ICC 0.98 between algorithms; uncertainty related to volume, vessel attachment and surface area
relevance: Recent evidence that repeatability is algorithm-specific for small lesions
not_established: Abstract only; same-session repeats; lung

citation: Rothe JH, Grieser C, Lehmkuhl L, Schnapauff D, Fernandez CP, Maurer MH, Mussler A, Hamm B, Denecke T, Steffen IG. Size determination and response assessment of liver metastases with computed tomography - comparison of RECIST and volumetric algorithms. Eur J Radiol 2013;82(11):1831-1839.
venue_and_status: European Journal of Radiology, published; abstract read
problem: Volumetric algorithms vs RECIST for liver metastases
method: Three 3D algorithms and RECIST-based volume; three repeats by one observer; follow-up subset
data: 102 liver metastases in 45 patients (pancreatic cancer n=22, colon cancer n=23); follow-up of 55 metastases in 29 patients
main_result: Intraobserver variability 0.6-10.8% (seeded region growing), 0.4-13.7% (slice segmentation), 3.6-32.8% (RECIST and threshold); response classification discordant in 10-21% of patients between methods
relevance: Liver metastases including pancreatic-cancer metastases (as in PanTrack); method choice altered response categories
not_established: Abstract only; no repeat scans; single observer

citation: Wulff AM, Bolte H, Fischer S, Freitag-Wolf S, Soza G, Tietjen C, Biederer J, Heller M, Fabel M. Lung, liver and lymph node metastases in follow-up MSCT: comprehensive volumetric assessment of lesion size changes. RoFo 2012;184(9):820-828.
venue_and_status: RoFo, published; abstract read
problem: Precision and inter-rater variability of volumetric follow-up of metastases
method: Three readers; semi-automated volumetry vs RECIST 1.1
main_result: Inter-reader median variation coefficients 2.9-8.2% (volumetric) vs 9.4-12.8% (manual); limits of agreement +/-9.8 to +/-11.2% for volumetric assessment; volumes were converted to effective diameters
relevance: Organ-specific (liver, lymph node) reader variability of follow-up volumetry
not_established: Abstract only; reported scale appears to be effective diameter, not volume; check before citing

citation: Nishino M, Guo M, Jackman DM, DiPiro PJ, Yap JT, Ho TK, Hatabu H, Janne PA, Van den Abbeele AD, Johnson BE. CT tumor volume measurement in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer: performance characteristics of an emerging clinical tool. Acad Radiol 2011;18(1):54-62.
venue_and_status: Academic Radiology, published; abstract read
problem: Inter- and intraobserver variability of CT tumour volume
method: Two radiologists, commercial software
main_result: Interobserver 95% LoA for volume -26.0% to 18.6% (same scans)
relevance: Reader (same-scan) variability benchmark; not recommended for the revision
not_established: Abstract only; not scan-rescan

citation: Versteijne E, Gurney-Champion OJ, van der Horst A, Lens E, Kolff MW, Buijsen J, Ebrahimi G, Neelis KJ, Rasch CR, Stoker J, van Herk M, Bel A, van Tienhoven G. Considerable interobserver variation in delineation of pancreatic cancer on 3DCT and 4DCT: a multi-institutional study. Radiat Oncol 2017;12(1):58.
venue_and_status: Radiation Oncology, published; abstract read
problem: Interobserver variation of pancreatic tumour delineation
method: Eight radiation oncologists, four patients
data: Four patients with (borderline) resectable pancreatic cancer
main_result: Ratio of largest to smallest delineated GTV 6.8 (3DCT) and 16.5 (4DCT iGTV); overall observer SD 0.63 cm (GTV)
relevance: Only pancreas-specific variability evidence found; context for reference-annotation noise, not a repeatability benchmark
not_established: Radiotherapy delineation; abstract only; not recommended

citation: Oxnard GR, Zhao B, Sima CS, Ginsberg MS, James LP, Lefkowitz RA, Guo P, Kris MG, Schwartz LH, Riely GJ. Variability of lung tumor measurements on repeat computed tomography scans taken within 15 minutes. J Clin Oncol 2011;29(23):3114-3119.
venue_and_status: Journal of Clinical Oncology, published; abstract read
problem: Variability of tumour diameter on immediate re-imaging
